The best chain is QB11-QB12-QB7. QB12 sits in the middle. The product of its two CZ fidelities is 0.99852.

How I picked it: I read the current default calibration of the real garnet QPU (calibration set 9069c4ef-7ab6-4e50-be4f-c91d71c3a06d). It lists an IRB CZ fidelity for all 30 CZ pairs. I checked every chain of 3 connected qubits and multiplied its two fidelities. The QB11-QB12 pair has fidelity 0.999454 and the QB12-QB7 pair has 0.999066. Their product is 0.998520. The next best chain is QB11-QB12-QB17, with a product of 0.998175.

What I ran: I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly QB11, QB12 and QB7. It has a rotation on each qubit, a CZ on QB12-QB11, a CZ on QB12-QB7, and one more rotation each on QB11 and QB7. Then it measures all 3 qubits. I read the circuit back from the server. It has 2 CZ gates, both on the chosen pairs, and it measures QB11, QB12 and QB7. I simulated it without noise first. A perfect machine would give 000 half the time and 111 half the time, and never anything else.

Result: job 01a16486-e706-70c5-b6f4-bb4c2fd8a578 ran on garnet:mock with 200 shots and cost 0 credits. The counts are 000: 56, 011: 53, 100: 46, 111: 45 (bits in the order QB11, QB12, QB7).

What the numbers show: the mock does not simulate the circuit. It returns random bitstrings, so the 011 and 100 results do not come from the physics. A real GHZ run would show almost only 000 and 111. That would mean the 3 qubits are entangled, because measuring one qubit fixes the other two. The run shows that the circuit is valid on these qubits and that the server accepts it. The principle is that you place a circuit on the qubit pairs with the best measured gate quality. The chance that both CZ gates work is about the product of their fidelities, so the chain with the highest product should give the cleanest GHZ state on the real machine.
